analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import up to a 90-day supply of prescription drugs for personal use.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate health committee in July 2001 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law so individual Americans could legally buy prescription drugs from abroad — by mail or in personal baggage — up to a 90-day supply for their own use, not for resale. Drugs would have to be approved by the FDA-equivalent process, made in registered facilities, and come from countries whose safety rules are comparable to the U.S. The Health and Human Services Secretary would publish a public list of approved foreign-made drugs and collect import records. The goal was to let Americans buy the same medicines at the lower prices charged in other countries.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs — especially seniors and people on fixed incomes who take long-term medications. The bill would have let them buy the same FDA-approved drugs from countries where prices are lower, potentially saving hundreds or thousands of dollars a year on a 90-day supply.

how_it_helps.text: Permits individuals to import a personal-use, 90-day supply of prescription drugs by mail or in personal baggage, as long as the drug is legally dispensed in the country of origin and meets safety conditions.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to maintain and publicly post a list of approved drugs made in registered establishments outside the U.S. — or U.S.-made drugs exported abroad — so consumers can verify what they are buying.

Builds in safety safeguards: drugs must be FDA-approved, in final finished dosage form from a registered manufacturer, accompanied by an import form identifying the buyer, seller, and prescriber, and subject to any additional conditions the Secretary sets.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which sell the same drugs at far higher prices in the U.S. than in Canada and Europe, would lose some U.S. sales. The Treasury would fund a modest HHS program (authorized at $1 million) to administer the list and recordkeeping.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs carry some safety risk: even with safeguards, the FDA would have limited ability to verify the contents of every foreign shipment, and the bill relies on a public list and import paperwork to keep out counterfeit or substandard products.

The limits could blunt the benefit: restricting imports to a 90-day personal-use supply at roughly 90-day intervals means households could not pool orders or resell, and conditions the Secretary 'determines necessary' could narrow the exception further.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households paying U.S. drug prices, the potential savings were large and the safeguards in the bill were reasonably serious — approved drugs, registered manufacturers, import documentation. The real cost falls on brand-name drug makers' U.S. revenue, not on consumers. The main genuine risk is drug safety, which the bill addressed with conditions rather than eliminating.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on July 24, 2001, with Sen. Debbie Stabenow as its sole cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the U.S. price structure that lets them charge Americans more than what the same medicines cost abroad stayed untouched. Patients who would have bought lower-priced imported drugs are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 24, 2001 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
against.what_they_did: Fought drug importation legislation as a threat to U.S. drug prices, part of a broader industry campaign that kept importation bills from advancing during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split is invisible in the record: both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by Democrats.

industries.note: U.S. patients pay among the world's highest prices for these drugs while the same products sell for less abroad; personal importation would have let Americans buy at foreign prices. The industry's interest in blocking such bills runs directly against patients who need cheaper medicine.

industries.industry: Foreign and mail-order pharmacies dispensing U.S.-approved drugs
industries.note: Legal personal importation by mail would have created a lawful customer base abroad for pharmacies dispensing FDA-approved drugs at lower prices.
